content: Approximately 1% of the maternal dose of this drug is transferred to breast milk. However, there is limited information available regarding the effects of this drug on breastfed infants. Combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) have the potential to reduce milk production in breastfeeding women. This reduction in milk supply can occur at any time but is less likely to happen once breastfeeding is well-established. When feasible, it is advisable for breastfeeding women to use alternative methods of contraception until they discontinue breastfeeding. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be carefully weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the therapy and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child, whether from the therapy itself or from the underlying maternal condition. In general, the use of this drug is considered acceptable during pregnancy. Controlled studies conducted in pregnant women have not demonstrated evidence of fetal risk. The pharmacokinetics of the drug include hepatic metabolism, with two inactive acid metabolites of drospirenone (DSRP) being identified. The half-life of ethinyl estradiol is approximately 24 hours, while the half-life of drospirenone is approximately 30 hours. The drug is excreted primarily through the urine (38-47% as inactive metabolites) and feces (17-20% as inactive metabolites).
